questions.text:
Suppose L={p,q,r,s,t} is a lattice represented by the following Hasse diagram:

For any [latex]x,y\in L[/latex] not necessarily distinct, [latex]x\vee y[/latex] and [latex]x\wedge y[/latex] are join and meet of x,y respectively. Let [latex]L^{3}=\{(x,y,z):x,y,z\in L\}[/latex] be the set of all ordered triplets of the elements of L. Let [latex]P_{r} [/latex] be the probability that an element [latex](x,y,z)\in L^{3}[/latex] chosen equiprobably satisfies [latex]x\vee (y \wedge z)=(x\vee y)\wedge (x\vee z)[/latex] . Then
questions.solution:
The lattice has bottom p, top t, and q, r, s incomparable in the middle (the diamond [latex]M_3[/latex]). It is not distributive.

- Fails for x, y, z = three different middle elements, e.g. [latex]q\vee(r\wedge s)=q\vee p=q[/latex] but [latex](q\vee r)\wedge(q\vee s)=t\wedge t=t[/latex]. There are 3! = 6 such triples.
- It holds for all other triples.

[latex]P_r=\frac{125-6}{125}=\frac{119}{125}[/latex], which lies between 1/5 and 1.

Answer: [latex]\frac15\lt P_r\lt1[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider the operations
[latex]f(X,Y,Z)=X'YZ+XY'+Y'Z'[/latex] and [latex] g(X,Y,Z)=X'YZ+X'YZ'+XY[/latex].
Which one of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
Post's theorem: a function alone is complete if it is not 0-preserving, not 1-preserving, not self-dual, not monotone and not linear.

f: f(0,0,0) = 1, f(1,1,1) = 0 (so also not monotone). f(0,0,1) = f(1,1,0) = 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not self-dual. Not linear (fitting [latex]1\oplus Y\oplus Z[/latex] from the first rows gives f(1,1,1) = 1, but it is 0). So {f} is complete.

g: g(0,0,0) = 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0-preserving, so {g} cannot produce 1 from 0s [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not complete.

Answer: Only {f} is functionally complete

questions.text: Let G be a connected planar graph with 10 vertices. If the number of edges on each face is three, then the number of edges in G is ___________.
questions.solution:
Each face has 3 edges and each edge lies on 2 faces: 3f = 2e.

Euler: [latex]v-e+f=2\Rightarrow10-e+\frac{2e}{3}=2\Rightarrow e=24[/latex]

Answer: 24

questions.text: Let [latex]a_{n}[/latex] represent the number of bit strings of length n containing two consecutive 1s. What is the recurrence relation for [latex]a_{n}[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Split by how the string starts:

- Starts with 0: the remaining n[latex]-[/latex]1 bits need 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]a_{n-1}[/latex]
- Starts with 10: the remaining n[latex]-[/latex]2 bits need 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]a_{n-2}[/latex]
- Starts with 11: already done, rest free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]2^{n-2}[/latex]

[latex]a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+2^{n-2}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]a_{n-2}+a_{n-1}+2^{n-2}[/latex]
